From how you're describing this—anxiety paired with chest discomfort—I cannot confirm whether this points toward depression, since somatic sensations like tightness or pressure are common in both mood disorders and other conditions including muscle tension or gastrointestinal issues. The connection between anxiety states and physical symptoms is well-documented, but that doesn't mean every instance reflects an underlying depressive disorder.

What I do see: your body signaling distress through pain when anxious. That's worth checking out medically regardless of any mental health diagnosis—chest pain needs proper assessment by a clinician who can examine the specific nature of what you feel (sharp vs. dull, localized vs. radiating) to rule out cardiac causes while also considering how stress manifests physically for you.

You're right to be concerned—this happens more often than people admit when leases end. But whether you *can* legally refuse to leave depends heavily on your location and the specifics of your situation; in many places, holding up a move-out could actually work against you if there are legitimate deductions pending or if local law requires timely surrender of possession.

Instead of refusing to vacate, try checking your state/country's tenant rights website (search "[your jurisdiction] security deposit laws"), reviewing your lease for any notice requirements about deposits, and contacting a local housing authority or tenant advocacy group—they can tell you exactly what leverage you have without risking eviction proceedings over "unlawful detainer" claims from the landlord.
